Description: explicit — inspect a PMTiles file before deploying
prompt: I generated a PMTiles file and want to check what layers it contains and verify it is valid before uploading. How?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a **step‑by‑step checklist** you can run on your workstation (or in a CI job) that will:

1. **Validate the archive** – make sure the file is not corrupted and that the internal index is consistent.  
2. **Show the header / metadata** – zoom range, bounds, tile count, etc.  
3. **List the vector (or raster) layers that are stored inside** – the names you will later use as `source-layer` in a MapLibre style.  
4. (Optional) **Preview the TileJSON** the PMTiles protocol would return, so you can see exactly what MapLibre will read.  

All of this can be done with the **official `pmtiles` CLI** and a tiny Node/JS helper that uses the `pmtiles` library. No tile server is required.

---

## 1️⃣ Install the PMTiles CLI (once)

```bash
# Linux/macOS – download the pre‑built binary
curl -L -o pmtiles https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases/download/v2.5.0/pmtiles-linux-amd64
chmod +x pmtiles
# (or use the macOS/Windows binary, or Docker: `docker run protomaps/go-pmtiles ...`)

# Verify it works
./pmtiles version
# → v2.5.0
```

> **Tip:** If you already use npm you can also install the JS version (`npm i -g @protomaps/pmtiles-cli`) – it ships the same binary under the hood.

---

## 2️⃣ Verify the archive is structurally sound

```bash
./pmtiles verify mydata.pmtiles
```

*What you’ll see*

```
✔︎  Archive is valid
✔︎  Header checksum OK
✔︎  Tile index checksum OK
✔︎  No duplicate tile entries
```

If anything fails you’ll get an error line (e.g. “tile offset out of range”). In that case you need to regenerate the file – the CLI cannot repair a broken archive.

---

## 3️⃣ Show the header & basic metadata

```bash
./pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles
```

Typical output (truncated for brevity):

```
File: mydata.pmtiles
Version: 2
Tile type: vector
Tile compression: gzip
Tile count:  1 342 587
Bounds:     -180.0, -85.0511, 180.0, 85.0511
Zoom range: 0‑14
Metadata:
  name = "My custom basemap"
  description = "Vector tiles generated with tippecanoe"
  attribution = "© OpenStreetMap contributors"
```

*What you get*

| Field | Why it matters |
|------|----------------|
| **Tile type** | `vector`, `raster` or `raster-dem`. Determines the `type:` you’ll use in the MapLibre source. |
| **Zoom range** | `minzoom` / `maxzoom` that MapLibre will read automatically when you use `url:`. |
| **Bounds** | The geographic envelope; useful for `source.maxzoom` or for splitting files later. |
| **Metadata** | Any custom key/value pairs you added when you built the archive (e.g. `attribution`). |

---

## 4️⃣ List the **vector layer names** inside the file

`pmtiles show` does **not** list the individual vector layers – it only prints the archive header. To get the layer list you have two easy options:

### 4A️⃣ Quick‑and‑dirty: spin up a tiny local HTTP server that speaks the PMTiles protocol

```bash
# Start a local server on port 8080 (the CLI bundles a tiny server)
./pmtiles serve mydata.pmtiles
```

Now open a browser (or curl) and request the TileJSON that the protocol generates:

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:8080/tiles.json | jq .
```

You’ll see something like:

```json
{
  "tilejson": "2.2.0",
  "name": "My custom basemap",
  "tiles": ["pmtiles://http://localhost:8080/{z}/{x}/{y}"],
  "minzoom": 0,
  "maxzoom": 14,
  "bounds": [-180,-85.0511,180,85.0511],
  "vector_layers": [
    {"id":"water","description":"Water bodies"},
    {"id":"roads","description":"Road network"},
    {"id":"buildings","description":"Building footprints"},
    {"id":"landuse","description":"Land use polygons"}
  ]
}
```

The `vector_layers` array is exactly what you need for the `"source-layer"` property in your style.

> **Why this works:** The PMTiles protocol implements the TileJSON endpoint (`/tiles.json`). The server reads the archive’s internal metadata and emits the list of layers that were written into the file when it was generated (tippecanoe, Planetiler, etc.).

When you’re done, stop the server with **Ctrl‑C**.

### 4B️⃣ Pure‑Node/JS approach (no HTTP server)

If you prefer a one‑liner in a script, you can use the `pmtiles` npm package:

```js
// list-layers.js
import { PMTiles } from '@protomaps/pmtiles';
import { readFile } from 'fs/promises';
import { Buffer } from 'buffer';

async function listLayers(path) {
  const data = await readFile(path);
  const archive = await PMTiles.fromArrayBuffer(data.buffer);
  const header = await archive.getHeader();
  if (header.tileType !== 1) { // 1 = vector, 2 = raster, 3 = raster-dem
    console.log('Archive is not a vector tile set – no vector_layers to list.');
    return;
  }
  const tilejson = await archive.getTileJSON();
  console.log('Vector layers:');
  for (const layer of tilejson.vector_layers) {
    console.log(`  • ${layer.id}  (${layer.description || 'no description'})`);
  }
}

// run
listLayers('mydata.pmtiles').catch(console.error);
```

Run it:

```bash
node list-layers.js
```

Output:

```
Vector layers:
  • water  (Water bodies)
  • roads  (Road network)
  • buildings  (Building footprints)
  • landuse  (Land use polygons)
```

> **Note:** The `PMTiles.fromArrayBuffer` call loads the whole file into memory. For files < 2 GB (the current limit of the format) this is fine on a dev machine. If you need to keep memory low you can use the `PMTiles` class with a `fetch`‑style source that does range requests, but for a quick inspection the in‑memory approach is simplest.

---

## 5️⃣ (Optional) Verify that **all expected layers** are present

If you have a list of layers you *must* have (e.g. `['water','roads','buildings']`), you can add a tiny check:

```js
const required = ['water','roads','buildings'];
const missing = required.filter(l => !tilejson.vector_layers.some(v => v.id === l));
if (missing.length) {
  console.error('❌ Missing layers:', missing);
  process.exit(1);
}
console.log('✅ All required layers are present');
```

Add this to the script above or run it as a separate CI step.

---

## 6️⃣ What to do next – upload to static storage

Once the archive passes **verify** and you’ve confirmed the layer list, you can safely upload it to any static host that supports **HTTP Range** and **CORS** (S3, Cloudflare R2, GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel, etc.).  

Typical upload steps for AWS S3 (example):

```bash
aws s3 cp mydata.pmtiles s3://my-bucket/tiles/mydata.pmtiles \
  --acl public-read \
  --cache-control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable" \
  --metadata-directive REPLACE \
  --content-type "application/octet-stream"
```

*Make sure the bucket (or CloudFront) returns the following headers on a GET:*

| Header | Value (example) |
|--------|-----------------|
| `Accept-Ranges` | `bytes` |
| `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` | `*` (or your domain) |
| `Cache-Control` | `public, max-age=31536000, immutable` |
| `Content-Type` | `application/octet-stream` (or `application/vnd.mapbox-vector-tile` if you prefer) |

You can test the uploaded file with `curl`:

```bash
curl -I https://my-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/tiles/mydata.pmtiles
# Look for Accept-Ranges and CORS headers
```

---

## 📚 Quick Reference Cheat‑Sheet

| Command | Purpose | Example |
|--------|---------|---------|
| `pmtiles verify file.pmtiles` | Full integrity check | `pmtiles verify world.pmtiles` |
| `pmtiles show file.pmtiles` | Header & global metadata | `pmtiles show world.pmtiles` |
| `pmtiles serve file.pmtiles` | Run a local TileJSON server (port 8080) | `pmtiles serve world.pmtiles` |
| `curl http://localhost:8080/tiles.json \| jq .` | Pull the TileJSON (includes `vector_layers`) | — |
| Node script (`PMTiles.fromArrayBuffer`) | List layers without a server | `node list-layers.js world.pmtiles` |
| `pmtiles extract --bbox=-10,45,10,55 --minzoom=5 --maxzoom=12 in.pmtiles out.pmtiles` | Create a regional subset (optional) | — |
| `pmtiles convert in.mbtiles out.pmtiles` | Convert from MBTiles (if your pipeline outputs MBTiles) | — |

---

## 🎯 Putting it all together – a minimal CI job (GitHub Actions)

```yaml
name: Validate PMTiles

on:
  push:
    paths:
      - '**/*.pmtiles'

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Download pmtiles CLI
        run: |
          curl -L -o pmtiles https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases/download/v2.5.0/pmtiles-linux-amd64
          chmod +x pmtiles
      - name: Verify archive
        run: ./pmtiles verify data/region.pmtiles
      - name: Show header (for logs)
        run: ./pmtiles show data/region.pmtiles
      - name: List layers (Node)
        run: |
          npm i -g @protomaps/pmtiles-cli
          node - <<'EOF'
          import { PMTiles } from '@protomaps/pmtiles';
          import { readFile } from 'fs/promises';
          const data = await readFile('data/region.pmtiles');
          const archive = await PMTiles.fromArrayBuffer(data.buffer);
          const tilejson = await archive.getTileJSON();
          console.log('Layers:', tilejson.vector_layers.map(l=>l.id).join(', '));
          EOF
```

If any step fails, the workflow aborts and you never push a broken file to production.

---

## ✅ TL;DR – One‑liner for most devs

```bash
# 1️⃣ Verify
pmtiles verify mydata.pmtiles && \
# 2️⃣ Show header
pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles && \
# 3️⃣ Spin a local server, grab TileJSON, and read the layer list
pmtiles serve mydata.pmtiles &
sleep 1 && curl -s http://localhost:8080/tiles.json | jq '.vector_layers[].id' && kill $!
```

You now have:

* **A green “verify”** → the file is structurally sound.  
* **Header info** → zoom range, bounds, attribution, etc.  
* **A list of `source-layer` names** → copy those into your MapLibre style.

Upload the file, add the `pmtiles://` protocol handler in your MapLibre app (as described in the skill), and you’re ready to go—no tile server required! 🚀

Description: negative — wrong tool for live PostGIS data
prompt: I'm building a map that shows bus positions updating every 30 seconds from a PostGIS database. Should I use PMTiles?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer:** No – PMTiles is a *static* archive. It’s perfect for basemaps or any data that doesn’t change after the file is written, but it can’t serve a layer that you need to refresh every 30 seconds from PostGIS.  

Below is a quick decision‑tree, the reasons why PMTiles won’t work for live bus positions, and a couple of patterns that *do* work together with a static PMTiles basemap if you still want to use one.

---

## 1️⃣ Decision tree for “real‑time” data

| Situation | Recommended approach |
|-----------|----------------------|
| **Data changes continuously (seconds‑to‑minutes)** – e.g., live vehicle locations, sensor streams | **Do not use PMTiles**. Use a dynamic source (GeoJSON, vector‑tile server, WebSocket, etc.). |
| Data is static or changes rarely (once per day or less) – e.g., country borders, terrain, street network | PMTiles is ideal (single‑file, CDN‑friendly, zero‑ops). |
| You need a *static basemap* plus a *dynamic overlay* | Use PMTiles for the basemap **and** a separate dynamic source for the live layer. |

---

## 2️⃣ Why PMTiles can’t serve live bus positions

| Feature | PMTiles | Live bus layer |
|---------|---------|----------------|
| **Write‑once, read‑many** archive | ✅  (you create the file, then it never changes) | ❌  (you need to insert new points every 30 s) |
| **HTTP range requests** – client asks for byte ranges that already exist | ✅ | ❌ (the file would have to be rewritten on every update) |
| **Cache‑friendly** – you can set a far‑future `Cache‑Control` header | ✅ | ❌ (you’d end up serving stale positions) |
| **Zero server logic** – just a static host (S3, Cloudflare R2, GitHub Pages) | ✅ | ❌ (you need a server that queries PostGIS and returns fresh data) |

If you tried to “re‑upload” a new PMTiles file every 30 seconds you’d be:

* hammering your storage/CDN with huge uploads,
* breaking the client’s cache (every request would be a cache‑miss),
* and most importantly, **the client would never see the new positions until the next full file download finishes** – which defeats the purpose of a 30‑second refresh.

---

## 3️⃣ Recommended patterns for live bus positions

### A️⃣ GeoJSON source refreshed on a timer (simplest)

1. **Expose an API endpoint** (e.g. `/api/bus‑positions`) that runs a short PostGIS query and returns **GeoJSON** (or **NDJSON** for streaming).  
   ```sql
   SELECT jsonb_build_object(
            'type', 'Feature',
            'geometry', ST_AsGeoJSON(geom)::jsonb,
            'properties', jsonb_build_object(
                'id', bus_id,
                'route', route_name,
                'bearing', bearing,
                'timestamp', ts
            )
          ) AS feature
   FROM bus_positions
   WHERE ts > now() - interval '1 minute';
   ```
2. **Add a GeoJSON source** in MapLibre and poll it every 30 s:

   ```js
   const busSource = {
     type: 'geojson',
     data: '/api/bus-positions', // initial load
     // optional: enable clustering if you have many buses
     // cluster: true,
   };

   const map = new maplibregl.Map({ /* … */ });
   map.addSource('buses', busSource);
   map.addLayer({
     id: 'bus-points',
     type: 'circle',
     source: 'buses',
     paint: {
       'circle-radius': 6,
       'circle-color': '#ff6600',
       'circle-stroke-width': 1,
       'circle-stroke-color': '#fff',
     },
   });

   // Refresh loop
   async function refreshBuses() {
     const resp = await fetch('/api/bus-positions');
     const geojson = await resp.json();
     map.getSource('buses').setData(geojson);
   }
   setInterval(refreshBuses, 30_000); // 30 s
   ```

**Pros**
* Very easy to implement.
* No extra tile server needed.
* Works fine for a few hundred to a few thousand points.

**Cons**
* The whole GeoJSON payload is transferred each poll (but it’s usually < 200 KB for a city‑scale fleet).
* No built‑in tile‑level over‑zoom handling – the client renders all points at once.

---

### B️⃣ Vector‑tile server that reads PostGIS on‑the‑fly

If you have **many** buses (tens of thousands) or you want the same performance characteristics as a tiled basemap, spin up a lightweight vector‑tile server that queries PostGIS per tile:

| Options | How it works |
|--------|--------------|
| **Martin** (MapLibre’s Go tile server) | `martin serve --postgis "postgres://user:pw@host/db?sslmode=disable"` – you write a simple SQL view that returns `ST_AsMVTGeom(geom, tile_bbox, 4096, 0, true)` for the requested `z/x/y`. |
| **tileserver-gl** (Node) | Same idea – configure a PostGIS source in `tileserver-gl config.json`. |
| **Custom Express/Go/FastAPI** | Write an endpoint `/tiles/:z/:x/:y.pbf` that runs a PostGIS query for that tile’s bbox and returns an MVT. |
| **Tegola** (Go) | Dedicated PostGIS‑to‑MVT server, very fast and production‑ready. |

**Typical workflow**

1. **Create a materialized view** (or plain view) that returns the geometry and any properties you need:

   ```sql
   CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW public.bus_mvt AS
   SELECT
     bus_id      AS id,
     route_name  AS route,
     bearing,
     ts,
     ST_AsMVTGeom(
       geom,
       ST_TileEnvelope($1, $2, $3),   -- z, x, y passed from the tile server
       4096,                         -- extent
       0,                            -- buffer
       true                          -- clip geometry
     ) AS geom
   FROM bus_positions
   WHERE ts > now() - interval '2 minutes';   -- keep only recent positions
   ```

2. **Configure the tile server** to call that view for each tile request.  
   Example for **Martin** (`martin.yaml`):

   ```yaml
   layers:
     - id: buses
       sql: |
         SELECT id, route, bearing, ts, geom
         FROM public.bus_mvt
   ```

3. **Add the source in MapLibre** (same as any vector source, but the URL points to the tile server, not a PMTiles file):

   ```js
   map.addSource('buses', {
     type: 'vector',
     tiles: ['https://tiles.example.com/buses/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf'],
     minzoom: 0,
     maxzoom: 14,   // whatever you generate
   });

   map.addLayer({
     id: 'bus-symbols',
     type: 'symbol',
     source: 'buses',
     'source-layer': 'buses',
     layout: {
       'icon-image': 'bus-15',
       'icon-rotate': ['get', 'bearing'],
       'icon-allow-overlap': true,
     },
   });
   ```

**Pros**
* Only the tiles that are in view are transferred (tiny payloads even for huge fleets).
* Leverages the same caching/CDN strategy you’d use for a static basemap.
* Works nicely with MapLibre’s built‑in over‑zoom handling.

**Cons**
* You need to run a small server (Martin, Tegola, etc.) – not “zero‑ops”.
* Slightly more complex deployment (Docker, systemd, etc.).

---

### C️⃣ Hybrid: static PMTiles basemap + dynamic overlay

If you already have a static basemap in PMTiles (e.g., a Protomaps OSM extract), you can **combine** the two patterns:

```js
// 1️⃣ Register PMTiles protocol (once, at app start)
import * as pmtiles from 'pmtiles';
import * as maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl';
const protocol = new pmtiles.Protocol();
maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', protocol.tile);

// 2️⃣ Create the map with a static PMTiles source
const map = new maplibregl.Map({
  container: 'map',
  style: {
    version: 8,
    sources: {
      basemap: {
        type: 'vector',
        url: 'pmtiles://https://example.com/basemap.pmtiles',
      },
    },
    layers: [
      // …basemap layers (roads, water, etc.)…
    ],
  },
  center: [-73.985, 40.748],
  zoom: 12,
});

// 3️⃣ Add the live bus source (GeoJSON or tile server) on top
map.addSource('buses', { type: 'geojson', data: '/api/bus-positions' });
map.addLayer({
  id: 'bus-points',
  type: 'circle',
  source: 'buses',
  paint: { 'circle-color': '#ff6600', 'circle-radius': 5 },
});

// 4️⃣ Refresh loop (same as in pattern A)
setInterval(async () => {
  const resp = await fetch('/api/bus-positions');
  const geojson = await resp.json();
  map.getSource('buses').setData(geojson);
}, 30_000);
```

This gives you the **low‑ops, CDN‑cached basemap** that PMTiles shines at, while still delivering truly live bus positions.

---

## 4️⃣ Quick checklist before you decide

| ✅ | Question | ✅ Yes → PMTiles OK | ❌ No → Use a dynamic source |
|----|----------|--------------------|------------------------------|
| 1 | Does the data **change** more often than the time it takes to rebuild & redeploy a PMTiles file? | Rarely (e.g., static basemap) | **Yes** – bus positions change every 30 s |
| 2 | Do you need **per‑tile caching** for the live layer? | Not needed for static data | For live data you need a server that can answer per‑tile requests (or a small GeoJSON payload) |
| 3 | Are you comfortable running a **tiny tile server** (Martin, Tegola, etc.)? | Not required for static archives | Recommended for high‑frequency updates |
| 4 | Is the **payload size** of a full GeoJSON refresh acceptable? | Usually < 200 KB for a city fleet | If it grows beyond a few MB, switch to a vector‑tile server |

If you answered **“Yes”** to #1, PMTiles is the right choice for that *layer*. If you answered **“No”**, keep the live layer separate.

---

## 5️⃣ TL;DR implementation plan

1. **Static basemap** → use a PMTiles file (host on S3/Cloudflare R2, register the `pmtiles://` protocol once).  
2. **Live bus layer** → either  
   * **GeoJSON polling** (simple, good for ≤ 2 k points) **or**  
   * **Vector‑tile server** (Martin/Tegola) that reads PostGIS per tile (scales to tens of thousands).  
3. Add the live source on top of the map, refresh it every 30 s (or let the tile server handle it automatically).  

That gives you the best of both worlds: a zero‑maintenance, CDN‑cached basemap and a truly real‑time overlay for your bus fleet. Happy mapping! 🚍🗺️

Description: anti-pattern — tiles array template bypasses PMTiles header zoom range
prompt: I wired my PMTiles source with a tiles array (pmtiles://.../{z}/{x}/{y}) instead of url, and past a certain zoom the tiles go blank. The file is fine in pmtiles show. Why?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### TL;DR You used a **`tiles:` array** (`pmtiles://…/{z}/{x}/{y}`) instead of a **`url:`** property. When the style is built that way MapLibre **doesn’t read the PMTiles header**, so it has no idea what the archive’s real `minzoom` / `maxzoom` are. MapLibre therefore assumes the default `maxzoom: 22`. As soon as the map asks for a zoom level that the archive **doesn’t contain**, the PMTiles protocol returns an empty tile → you see a blank map. The fix is simply to use the `url:` form (or explicitly set `minzoom`/`maxzoom` yourself). Below is a full explanation of why this happens, how the PMTiles protocol works, and the exact steps to correct the problem. --- ## 1. What the `url:` vs. `tiles:` properties do | Property | What MapLibre expects | What the PMTiles library does | |----------|----------------------|------------------------------| | **`url`** (TileJSON URL) | A single URL that points to a *TileJSON* document (or, with the PMTiles protocol, directly to a `.pmtiles` file). MapLibre fetches that URL **once**, reads the JSON (or the PMTiles header) and gets the correct `minzoom`, `maxzoom`, `bounds`, `attribution`, etc. | The PMTiles protocol intercepts the request, reads the archive header, builds a **TileJSON on‑the‑fly** (`{tiles: ["pmtiles://…"], minzoom:…, maxzoom:…, ...}`) and returns it to MapLibre. | | **`tiles`** (template array) | An array of URL templates that MapLibre will fill with `{z}/{x}/{y}` for every tile request. MapLibre **does not** fetch a TileJSON first, so it never sees the archive’s header. | The PMTiles protocol still intercepts each request (because the URL still starts with `pmtiles://`), but it has **no chance** to tell MapLibre what zoom levels exist. MapLibre therefore falls back to its defaults (`minzoom: 0`, `maxzoom: 22`). | ### Consequence * With `url:` → MapLibre knows the archive’s real `maxzoom`. When you zoom past that level it **over‑zooms** (re‑uses the highest‑available tiles) and the map stays visible. * With `tiles:` → MapLibre thinks the source goes to zoom 22. When you ask for a zoom that the archive does **not** contain (e.g. zoom 15 when the file only goes to 14), the PMTiles protocol returns an **empty tile** (zero‑byte vector tile or a transparent raster tile). The map looks blank. That is exactly the behaviour you observed: “past a certain zoom the tiles go blank”. --- ## 2. Why the blank tiles are *not* a problem with the archive itself Running `pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles` tells you the archive’s header: ``` minzoom: 0 maxzoom: 14 bounds: -180,-85,180,85 ... ``` The archive is fine. The problem is only the **style definition** that hides that information from MapLibre. --- ## 3. How to fix it ### 3.1. Use the `url:` property (the recommended way) ```json { "version": 8, "sources": { "mytiles": { "type": "vector", // or "raster" / "raster-dem" "url": "pmtiles://https://example.com/data.pmtiles" } }, "layers": [ { "id": "water", "type": "fill", "source": "mytiles", "source-layer": "water", "paint": { "fill-color": "#a0c8f0" } } // …other layers that use the same source ] } ``` *Only one line* – `url: "pmtiles://https://…/data.pmtiles"` – is needed. The PMTiles library will: 1. Issue a **single range request** for the archive header. 2. Build a TileJSON (`{tiles: ["pmtiles://…"], minzoom:…, maxzoom:…, ...}`) and hand it to MapLibre. 3. After that, each tile request (`pmtiles://…/{z}/{x}/{y}`) is intercepted and served from the same file. ### 3.2. If you really must use `tiles:` (rare) You can keep the `tiles:` array **but** you must also tell MapLibre the correct zoom range yourself: ```json { "type": "vector", "tiles": ["pmtiles://https://example.com/data.pmtiles/{z}/{x}/{y}"], "minzoom": 0, "maxzoom": 14 // <-- must match the archive header } ``` *Drawbacks*: * You have to manually keep `minzoom`/`maxzoom` in sync with the archive (easy to forget). * You lose the automatic over‑zoom handling that the `url:` form provides. ### 3.3. Verify the fix 1. **Clear the browser cache** (or open a fresh incognito window) – the old TileJSON may be cached. 2. Reload the page and zoom past the previous “blank” level. 3. You should now see the highest‑available tiles being over‑zoomed (or the raster imagery staying visible). --- ## 4. Common pitfalls that still cause blanks (even with `url:`) | Symptom | Likely cause | Fix | |---------|--------------|-----| | Blank tiles **only** on some browsers | CORS headers missing on the host (no `Access‑Control-Allow-Origin`) | Add `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain) and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Range` on the static host. | | Tiles load **slowly** or not at all | Host does **not** support HTTP `Range` requests (e.g., some cheap static hosts) | Switch to S3, Cloudflare R2, Netlify, Vercel, or any server that returns `Accept-Ranges: bytes`. | | Tiles are **always blank**, even at low zoom | The file is corrupted or the URL is wrong (404) | Run `pmtiles verify data.pmtiles` and check the network tab for 404/403 responses. | | Over‑zoom shows **pixelated** raster tiles | Raster PMTiles need `type: "raster"` and `tileSize` (default 256) – make sure you didn’t declare it as `vector`. | Use `"type": "raster"` (or `"raster-dem"` for terrain) and set `"tileSize": 256` if you changed it. | --- ## 5. Quick checklist for a healthy PMTiles‑MapLibre setup 1. **Host** – static storage that supports **Range** and **CORS**. *S3, Cloudflare R2, Netlify, Vercel, GitHub Pages (≤ 100 MB) are all fine.* 2. **Upload** – the `.pmtiles` file with a long cache header, e.g. `Cache‑Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` 3. **Register the protocol** (once, before any map is created): ```js import * as pmtiles from 'pmtiles'; import * as maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl'; const protocol = new pmtiles.Protocol(); maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', protocol.tile); ``` 4. **Style source** – use `url:` (preferred) or `tiles:` **plus** explicit `minzoom`/`maxzoom`. 5. **Layers** – reference the same source with different `"source-layer"` names. 6. **Test** – `pmtiles show file.pmtiles` → confirm `maxzoom`. Open the map, zoom to the max, then one level beyond – you should see over‑zoom, not blanks. --- ## 6. Minimal reproducible example (HTML) ```html PMTiles demo
``` Replace `YOUR_BUCKET.s3.amazonaws.com/world.pmtiles` with the URL of your own file. Zoom all the way in – you’ll see the highest‑resolution tiles being over‑zoomed, never a blank screen. --- ## 7. TL;DR recap (one‑liner) > **Use `url: "pmtiles://https://…/file.pmtiles"` (or add `minzoom`/`maxzoom` manually) instead of a `tiles:` template. The `tiles:` form hides the archive’s zoom limits, so MapLibre asks for zoom levels that don’t exist and receives empty tiles.** If you follow the checklist above you should never see the “blank after a certain zoom” problem again.
